title: Ting Et Al. - 2025 - Astro Mlab5
chunk_summaries: AstroMLab 5 focuses on creating structured summaries and extracting concepts from a vast collection of 400,000 astrophysics papers. The project involves contributions from researchers Yuan-Sen Ting (The Ohio State University), Alberto Accomazzi (Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics), Tirthankar Ghosal (Oak Ridge National Laboratory), Tuan Dung Nguyen (University of Pennsylvania), Rui Pan (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign), Zechang Sun (Tsinghua University), and Tijmen de Haan (KEK).

The dataset comprises 408,590 astrophysics papers from arXiv (astro-ph) covering the period from 1992 to July 2025. It features structured summaries divided into six sections (Background, Motivation, Methodology, Results, Interpretation, Implication) and includes the extraction of 9,999 unique concepts with detailed descriptions. The dataset contains 3.8 million paper-concept associations and semantic embeddings for all concepts, offering denser coverage and a more uniform distribution compared to traditional ADS keywords. The analysis of the embedding space shows that concepts are semantically dispersed, facilitating discovery through various entry points. The concept vocabulary and embeddings are publicly available at https://github.com/tingyuansen/astro-ph_knowledge_graph.

The deployment of large language models (LLMs) as autonomous agents for reasoning about scientific literature and executing research tasks is advancing, particularly in fields like materials science and chemistry. However, the astronomy literature lacks well-curated text resources, as existing databases are either overly comprehensive or too sparse, limiting effective analysis. Keywords, intended to bridge this gap, often lack mapping to controlled vocabularies and are inconsistently distributed across papers. To enhance the utility of LLMs in astronomy, a centralized effort is proposed to create structured summaries and concepts from all astro-ph papers, building on recent advancements in domain-specific models and knowledge graph construction. This initiative aims to provide a comprehensive dataset of 408,590 papers and 9,999 unique concepts, facilitating better access to structured knowledge representations for research.

The process of converting astrophysics PDFs to machine-readable text faces challenges due to mathematical equations, multi-column layouts, and figures with captions. The chosen method is OCR, as LaTeX source files are inconsistently structured and often use custom macros. Initially, the pipeline utilized Nougat (Blecher et al., 2023), which converts PDFs to markdown format, requiring about 1 minute per paper on a V100 GPU and totaling around 6,000 GPU-hours for over 350,000 papers. In November 2024, the transition to Mathpix OCR API was made for its greater reliability, as Nougat occasionally produced repetitive text on 1 in 500 pages. Both OCR methods preserve mathematical notation in LaTeX format, with Nougat using markdown headers and Mathpix retaining LaTeX section commands. Inspections of Mathpix's output for approximately 50,000 papers showed no systematic errors affecting summary quality.

The text discusses a multi-stage summarization approach for processing academic papers, focusing on a chunk-based compression method. Early attempts to summarize entire papers resulted in incomplete and superficial outputs, prompting the development of a strategy that divides papers into approximately 10,000-character segments at section boundaries. This method ensures coherence by maintaining context across chunks, despite increased token costs. The compression system prioritizes retaining LaTeX formulas, emphasizing motivations, methods, key results, and technical jargon while excluding acknowledgments and references. As language models improved, various models like GPT-4o and DeepSeek-v3 were utilized, leading to over $50,000 in API costs for summarizing 408,590 papers. Additionally, raw summaries are reorganized into seven structured sections—Title and Author, Background, Motivation, Methodology, Results, Interpretation, and Implication—to enhance systematic analysis and knowledge representation.

The text outlines a methodology for extracting and constructing a vocabulary of key concepts from organized summaries using a language model (LLM). The process aims to identify approximately 10 novel concepts per paper, focusing on innovations in both scientific and technological domains while avoiding generic terms. Each concept consists of a concise name, a classification (e.g., Cosmology, High Energy Astrophysics), and a detailed description. To ensure consistency, a multi-stage clustering process is employed to merge semantically similar concepts, resulting in a final vocabulary of 9,999 concepts after manual review. The distribution of these concepts across various research categories is provided, highlighting their statistical robustness and contextual richness compared to traditional keyword systems. The methodology emphasizes the importance of scrutiny when utilizing the dataset for specific applications.

The evaluation of a new concept vocabulary for academic papers, compared to traditional ADS keywords from the NASA ADS API, reveals significant advantages in coverage and frequency distribution. Traditional ADS keywords, which are author-supplied and lack systematic curation, show high sparsity, with many papers having only a few keywords, limiting their effectiveness for semantic search and recommendation systems. In contrast, the new vocabulary achieves complete coverage of all 408,590 papers, averaging 9.4 concepts per paper, and maintains a balanced frequency distribution that avoids the extremes of overly broad or overly specific terms. This systematic curation allows for meaningful thematic identification across various research areas, including emerging topics like deep learning in astronomy. Additionally, concepts are shown to be superior to abstracts for discovery tasks, as they capture diverse ideas embedded within papers that abstracts may overlook. The analysis of embedding spaces demonstrates that concepts provide a broader semantic context, facilitating the discovery of relevant research even when specific terms are not mentioned in abstracts. Overall, the new vocabulary offers a robust alternative for enhancing semantic search and recommendation algorithms in academic research.

The text discusses the applications of a concept vocabulary in analyzing the temporal evolution of concepts and co-occurrence of research themes in astrophysics. It highlights how the vocabulary allows for precise tracking of idea emergence and connections across research areas, illustrated by a temporal analysis showing a decline in new concept emergence in recent years, attributed to field maturation and clustering biases. A notable peak in 2007 coincided with changes in arXiv's cross-listing policies, leading to the introduction of theoretical physics concepts into astrophysics. The analysis also reveals that deep learning has dominated recent concept emergence, with significant contributions from various astronomical applications. Additionally, co-occurrence analysis, using the Ochiai coefficient, provides insights into how concepts interconnect, showing increased integration of computational methods with traditional astrophysical domains over time. The findings indicate a shift towards data-intensive research, while established domains maintain stable structures. Overall, the concept vocabulary facilitates a quantitative study of the evolution of astrophysics research, revealing patterns of computational integration and methodological shifts.

The dataset, available on GitHub at https://github.com/tingyuansen/astro-ph_knowledge_graph, encompasses all astro-ph papers from 1992 to July 2025. It emphasizes concept vocabulary and embeddings for reproducibility and downstream applications, while structured summaries follow a conservative distribution policy. The public release includes a CSV of concept vocabulary with labels, names, classes, and descriptions; concept embeddings using text-embedding-3-large; paper metadata such as year, arXiv ID, and ADS bibcodes; and Python scripts for data handling. Additionally, a citation network from the NASA ADS API is provided, featuring 1.67 million unique identifiers for both internal and external citations. Dataset statistics are summarized in Table 4.

This work introduces a comprehensive dataset of 408,590 astrophysics papers from arXiv (1992-2025), featuring structured six-section summaries, 9,999 AI-generated concepts with detailed descriptions, and semantic embeddings. The dataset addresses the limitations of traditional keyword systems by providing a systematically generated concept vocabulary that ensures consistent coverage and balanced distributions across all papers. Each concept captures dispersed semantic information, enhancing scientific discovery beyond what abstracts can offer. Temporal analysis reveals the evolution of the field, particularly the rise of machine learning from 2015-2025, and highlights the integration of computational methods with traditional astrophysics. The dataset supports applications such as semantic search, research trend analysis, and knowledge graph construction, facilitating AI-assisted scientific discovery. All code and data processing pipelines are publicly available, and the research is supported by various grants and computational resources. Future work will focus on extrinsic evaluations and integration with recommender systems for improved paper discovery.

This appendix presents a structured summary format for academic papers, emphasizing a comprehensive organization across six semantic sections: Background, Motivation, Methodology, Results, Interpretation, and Implication. The example provided focuses on the study of USco1606-1935, a candidate low-mass binary system identified using 2MASS data, which aims to enhance understanding of multiple star formation. The methodology involved photometric and astrometric analysis, confirming the binary nature of USco1606-1935 A and its potential association with B. Results indicated a high probability of a bound binary system, although caution is advised due to the possibility of chance alignments. The implications suggest that if confirmed as gravitationally bound, USco1606-1935 would be a rare example of a young multiple system, highlighting the need for systematic searches in similar stellar environments. Additionally, the text discusses the emergence of new concepts in astrophysics from 2015-2025, noting a trend towards building connections between established ideas rather than introducing entirely new topics, with a significant focus on machine learning applications. Co-occurrence analysis reveals thematic structures within research domains, illustrating both within-domain specialization and cross-domain methodological connections.

This strategy ensures coherence across chunks while prioritizing the retention of LaTeX formulas, key motivations, methods, results, and technical jargon, while excluding acknowledgments and references.

A key aspect of the methodology involves extracting and constructing a vocabulary of key concepts from these organized summaries using a language model. The process aims to identify around 10 novel concepts per paper, focusing on innovations in both scientific and technological domains while avoiding generic terms. Each concept is defined by a concise name, a classification—such as Cosmology or High Energy Astrophysics—and a detailed description. To ensure consistency, a multi-stage clustering process merges semantically similar concepts, resulting in a final vocabulary of 9,999 concepts after manual review. The distribution of these concepts across various research categories highlights their statistical robustness and contextual richness compared to traditional keyword systems, emphasizing the importance of scrutiny when utilizing the dataset for specific applications.

With 3.8 million paper-concept associations and semantic embeddings for all concepts, the dataset offers denser coverage and a more uniform distribution than traditional ADS keywords. Notably, the analysis of the embedding space reveals that concepts are semantically dispersed, enhancing the potential for discovery through various entry points. The concept vocabulary and embeddings are publicly accessible, providing valuable resources for further research at https://github.com/tingyuansen/astro-ph_knowledge_graph. This initiative ultimately aims to facilitate better access to structured knowledge representations for research in the field of astrophysics.

A significant challenge in this endeavor is converting astrophysics PDFs into machine-readable text, complicated by the presence of mathematical equations, multi-column layouts, and figures with captions. To address this, the project employs Optical Character Recognition (OCR) methods, as LaTeX source files are often inconsistently structured and utilize custom macros. Initially, the pipeline utilized Nougat (Blecher et al., 2023), which converts PDFs to markdown format, requiring about one minute per paper on a V100 GPU and totaling around 6,000 GPU-hours for over 350,000 papers. In November 2024, the project transitioned to the Mathpix OCR API for its greater reliability, as Nougat occasionally produced repetitive text on one in every 500 pages. Both OCR methods effectively preserve mathematical notation in LaTeX format, with Nougat using markdown headers and Mathpix retaining LaTeX section commands. Inspections of Mathpix's output for approximately 50,000 papers showed no systematic errors affecting summary quality, thereby ensuring the integrity of the structured summaries being developed. As language models improved, various models like GPT-4o and DeepSeek-v3 were utilized, leading to over $50,000 in API costs for summarizing the extensive dataset. Additionally, raw summaries are reorganized into the seven structured sections to enhance systematic analysis and knowledge representation.

The concept vocabulary not only surpasses traditional keywords in coverage and distribution but also proves superior for discovery tasks, capturing diverse ideas embedded within papers that abstracts may overlook. Furthermore, the vocabulary enables a quantitative analysis of the temporal evolution of concepts and the co-occurrence of research themes in astrophysics. Deep learning has emerged as a dominant theme in recent concept emergence, significantly impacting various astronomical applications. Co-occurrence analysis, utilizing the Ochiai coefficient, illustrates how concepts interconnect, showing an increased integration of computational methods with traditional astrophysical domains over time.
